strengths: Well-motivated and clearly positioned new task: reference-video-driven temporal effect transfer (Ref Video + Input Video → Output Video) is genuinely distinct from text-based or keyframe-conditioned editing, and the paper is plausibly the first systematic treatment of it.

The dataset contribution is substantial and well-engineered: a scalable V2V pair-creation pipeline (image generation → pose/last-frame anchoring → conditional video generation) that produces motion-consistent effect pairs, combined with LoRA-derived I2V data and programmatic effects, yielding 120K+ triplets over 1,700 effects. The data pipeline is the paper's strongest technical contribution and the appendix documents it thoroughly (hyperparameter tables, effect catalogs).

Comprehensive evaluation including a sizeable human preference study (669/455/252 annotations across V2V, I2V, and code-based effects) with sensible dimensions (Reference Video Adherence, Input Video Adherence), plus embedding-based similarity metrics and VBench-style quality measures. The authors are candid that existing metrics only partially capture the task, which supports the reliance on human judgment.

Useful practical capability: disentangled classifier-free guidance over text, input video, and reference effect (Eq. 1–5) enables user control over edit strength, demonstrated qualitatively in Figure 8.
Honest limitations section: failure cases (Fig. 9), human-centric data bias, and ~2x inference cost are all explicitly acknowledged.
weaknesses: Distributional circularity between training data and evaluation: V2V validation pairs are generated by the same pipeline (Sec. 3.2.2) as training data with only 'novel prompts', and the code-based evaluation uses 'the same families of operations and transitions' as training. Thus the headline generalization claims are weaker than they appear — the strongest test of true generalization (unseen LoRA effects on novel videos) is the smallest subset, and even those effects come from the same community LoRA ecosystem as training.

The dataset is almost entirely model-generated (LoRAs, Qwen Image Edit, Wan VACE, GPT-4o prompts), raising concerns about compounding artifacts, prompt/LoRA trigger tokens leaking into conditioning, and whether the model learns effects or the stylistic priors of the specific generator stack. No analysis of quality filtering or error rates in the generated pairs is provided.

Baseline comparisons are inherently uneven: all baselines (Wan I2V, VACE, Lucy Edit) receive only text descriptions of effects and cannot condition on the reference video. The large win-rate margins (78–98%) partly reflect this asymmetry rather than architectural superiority; a stronger control would have been useful.

The conditioning-input-similarity metrics have no ground truth and are acknowledged to be imperfect proxies; baselines' higher input similarity is interpreted as 'under-editing', but this interpretation is not independently validated.

Architectural novelty is modest: the method is a fairly direct extension of Wan's channel-concatenated conditioning to an extra reference video stream (doubling token count), trained as LoRA fine-tuning. The core ML contribution is data curation, which is valuable but should be recognized as such; there is no ablation isolating the contribution of each data source (LoRA vs. V2V pipeline vs. code-based) to final performance.

User study protocol is under-specified in the main text: number of raters, whether reference and input videos were shown during rating, and the meaning of the ±2 mean-score scale are deferred to the supplement; without these details the reported win rates are hard to fully assess.

The claim of being 'tuning-free' is potentially misleading — the system requires significant training (10K steps on 8 A100s); it is tuning-free only at inference time. Also unclear whether the dataset itself will be released, which affects reproducibility of the benchmark claim.
Attribution considerations for the 43 community-sourced Hugging Face LoRAs used to build and evaluate the dataset (and the Senorita source videos) deserve more explicit discussion of licensing.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely new task — reference-based transfer of temporally evolving video effects — and the claim of being first on this Ref+Input->Output video setup appears credible given the related work coverage.

The data contribution is substantial and non-trivial: a 120K-triplet dataset spanning LoRA-derived I2V effects, a scalable V2V pair-creation pipeline (first/last-frame interpolation plus pose-conditioned generation), and programmatic code-based effects, with detailed hyperparameter documentation in the supplement.

The conditioning architecture is a sensible, well-motivated extension of the Wan FLF2V channel-concatenation design, and the multi-directional classifier-free guidance (text, input video, reference effect) with normalization is a useful practical contribution for controllable editing.

Evaluation is multi-pronged: pairwise human studies across three task settings with reasonably large annotation counts (669/455/252), embedding-similarity metrics, and VBench-style statistics, plus a limitations section with a concrete failure example and honest discussion of doubled inference cost.
Qualitative results (Figs. 6-7) are convincing for the motivating use cases, showing temporal effects (camera motion, gradual morphing) that text-only baselines clearly fail to reproduce.
weaknesses: Evaluation circularity is the most serious concern. The V2V validation set is generated with the exact same pipeline (Sec. 3.2.2) as the training data, differing only in prompts, and the code-based test set shares the same operation families and transitions as training, varying only hyperparameters. Thus the headline 'generalizes to unseen effect categories' claim is weakly supported: the model is largely tested in-distribution. The 28 unseen LoRA effects are a much smaller and partly anecdotal test.

The dataset composition (roughly 100K of 120K triplets from deterministic code-based effects) raises the concern that the model learns mostly low-level, programmatically compositable effects, while the truly hard, semantically rich V2V effects rest on a much smaller, model-generated (Qwen/Flux/WAN-distilled) subset. No ablation on data mixture contribution is provided, so the source of the gains is unclear.

Training data is generated by the same family of models the method builds on (Wan VACE, Wan FLF2V, Qwen Image), creating a distillation-loop risk: the model may inherit and amplify artifacts of the generator, and the ceiling on achievable effect quality is bounded by the data pipeline's generators. This is discussed nowhere in the paper.

The title's 'tuning-free' is misleading: the model is fine-tuned with LoRAs for 10K steps; only inference is tuning-free. This phrasing overstates novelty relative to per-effect LoRA baselines it criticizes.

The human study design is under-specified in the main paper (annotator screening, number of annotators, interface, how ablations were blinded), and the reported win-rate ranges (e.g., 70-98%) aggregate very different comparisons, including against the authors' own ablations, which inflates apparent superiority. No significance testing is reported.

The quantitative metrics are weak proxies: VideoPrism/CLIP similarity to the reference video cannot distinguish temporal-dynamics transfer from static appearance copying (Table 3 even shows the method loses on first-frame similarity), and the authors themselves concede existing metrics 'only partially reflect' the task — yet no better temporal-adherence metric is proposed.

Baselines are structurally disadvantaged: all baselines receive only text descriptions of the effects, so the comparison mostly demonstrates that reference conditioning helps (expected) rather than that this particular architecture or dataset is superior. A reference-image/keyframe-conditioned baseline or a Dynamic-Concepts-style comparison is missing.

Several presentation issues undermine polish: the 'first to show results on this task' claim is repeated loosely, Table 3's first-frame similarity result is under-interpreted, the abstract promises a 'benchmark' that is partly model-generated rather than a community-standard evaluation, and the code-based Dynamic degree for the method (0.143 vs 0.190 baseline in Table 10) goes unremarked despite indicating less dynamic output.

Reproducibility is uncertain: the dataset pipelines depend on multiple proprietary/heavyweight models (GPT-4o for effect generation, Flux Kontext, Qwen Image Edit) and the release statement is only 'code will be released upon publication,' with no explicit dataset release commitment.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated task: the paper is, to the best of my knowledge, the first to formulate and demonstrate reference-video-conditioned temporal effect transfer (Ref Video + Input -> Output) in a feed-forward manner, going beyond text-prompt or keyframe-conditioned editing.

The dataset contribution is substantial and creative: over 120K triplets spanning 1,700 effects, assembled from three complementary sources (LoRA-derived I2V, an automated V2V pair-generation pipeline, and programmatic code-based effects). The V2V pair-creation pipeline (Figure 4) that couples first/last-frame conditioning with per-frame pose conditioning is a clever, scalable solution to a genuinely hard data problem.

Comprehensive evaluation across three tasks (I2V, neural V2V, code-based V2V) with both automatic embedding-similarity metrics and a sizable human preference study (669/455/252 annotations), including a 'No Ref' ablation and per-dimension (reference adherence vs. input adherence) analysis, which is appropriate for this subjective task.
The multi-source CFG guidance (Eq. 1-5) for controlling reference vs. input adherence is a practical addition, and inference-time control is demonstrated qualitatively (Figure 8).

The paper is clearly written, the architecture extension of Wan FLF2V conditioning is well explained, and limitations (occlusion handling, human-centric dataset bias, 2x inference cost) are candidly discussed in the supplement. Code release is promised and a supplementary website with extensive video results is provided.
weaknesses: Evaluation circularity risk: the neural V2V validation set is generated by the same pipeline (Sec 3.2.2) and the code-based validation set uses the same effect/transition families as training, so the model is evaluated largely on data drawn from its own training distribution rather than on real-world ground-truth effects. The unseen generalization claims would be much stronger if evaluated on authentic (non-generated) reference effect videos with human-verified outputs.

All baselines are text-only; no baseline that conditions on any reference signal is compared. The dominant conclusion 'reference conditioning helps' is somewhat expected, and the comparison conflates the conditioning signal with the 120K-triplet fine-tuning. A stronger baseline (e.g., few-shot conditioning via concatenated frames, or image-reference editing models applied per-frame) is missing.

Training data quality ceilings: a large fraction of the training targets are themselves outputs of generative models (LoRA I2V outputs, the V2V pipeline), so RefVFX largely distills these generators; the paper does not analyze how generator artifacts propagate to the model, and the human-study win rates (78-98%) seem implausibly high, suggesting possible annotator bias (e.g., sharper/more vivid outputs winning regardless of effect fidelity).

Some quantitative evidence is mixed and under-discussed: in Table 3, Ours has the lowest First Frame Sim (0.7698 vs. 0.7911), and in Table 4 the method has lower Input Sim than VACE Depth, which the paper attributes to 'under-editing' by baselines but does not disentangle from genuine content drift. Table 10 shows the method slightly underperforms on aesthetic and dynamic-degree metrics in several settings.

The code-based effect subset (posterize, pixelate, wipes, glitches) is comparatively simple and may dominate the 120K count (100K of ~120K triplets); the effective diversity of temporally rich, 'cinematic' effects is smaller than the headline numbers suggest, and the paper does not report per-source ablations (e.g., performance trained without each subset).

Scalability and reproducibility caveats: 480p/33-frame outputs only, 7 minutes per video on an A100, and dependence on many third-party generative components (Wan, Qwen-Image, Flux Kontext, GPT-4o) make exact reproduction difficult; the contribution is best viewed as Applied/Systems + Dataset rather than a general algorithmic advance.

strengths: Well-motivated and novel task formulation: reference-video-conditioned temporal effect transfer (Ref + Input → Output) is clearly distinct from existing prompt/keyframe-conditioned video editing, and the authors appear to be the first to demonstrate it in a feed-forward manner.

Substantial dataset contribution: over 120K triplets spanning 1,700+ effects from three complementary sources (LoRA-derived I2V, a scalable V2V pair-generation pipeline, and programmatic code-based effects). The V2V pair-creation pipeline (Fig. 4) that uses pose/first-last-frame conditioning to enforce motion-consistent edited pairs is a clever and reusable engineering contribution.

Thorough and well-designed evaluation: a large 2AFC user study (15,000+ annotations, 500+ annotators) with practice trials, randomization, and bootstrap confidence estimates; separated evaluation of neural V2V, code-based V2V, and I2V; plus VBench-style metrics and an interpretable multi-directional classifier-free guidance scheme (Eq. 1–5) that enables controllable trade-off between input fidelity and effect strength (Fig. 8).

Honest treatment of evaluation limitations: the authors acknowledge that embedding-similarity metrics only partially capture effect transfer and appropriately rely primarily on human judgment, and they report the expected near-parity of input-adherence between their method and the No-Ref ablation.

Meaningful limitations discussion (fine-grained occlusions, human-centric data bias, doubled inference cost) with a concrete qualitative failure example (Fig. 9), and good supplementary detail on dataset construction, hyperparameters, and user-study protocol supporting reproducibility.
The No-Ref ablation convincingly shows the reference video conditioning itself drives the effect-transfer capability rather than merely the fine-tuned backbone.
weaknesses: Baseline comparison is inherently asymmetric: all baselines (Wan I2V, VACE, Lucy Edit) receive only text descriptions of the effect while the proposed method sees the reference video. While no reference-conditioned baseline exists, the large win-rate margins partly reflect this information asymmetry, and the paper does not discuss how much of the advantage comes from conditioning modality versus the learned transfer behavior.

Heavy reliance on synthetic/generated training data creates a potential synthetic-to-real gap: V2V pairs are produced by image editing on endpoint frames plus interpolation, which may bias the model toward endpoint-decomposable effects; the paper does not analyze whether performance degrades on real-world reference videos whose effects cannot be expressed this way, nor quantify the effect diversity actually present versus claimed 1,700 effects.

Quantitative evidence is weak in magnitude: reference-similarity gains over baselines are modest (e.g., Ref Sim. 0.7014 vs. 0.6852 for Lucy Edit in Table 4; 0.7378 vs. 0.7230 in Table 3), and the paper concedes these metrics are imperfect proxies. There is no objective measure that specifically verifies temporal dynamics transfer (e.g., timing/rhythm alignment to the reference).

Risk of shortcut learning is not examined: since the model also receives the text prompt describing the effect (implicit in reference videos during training), it is unclear to what extent the model transfers the reference's dynamics versus following text; a No-Text or conflicting-text experiment would strengthen the case that reference conditioning is doing the temporal work.

Generalization claims rest on a small evaluation set (~56 reference videos for I2V, ~100 V2V instances), mostly human-centric, which limits the statistical strength of the unseen-category generalization claim.
Practical cost is significant: doubled inference time (~7 min/video on an A100) and a 14B-parameter backbone; the paper offers no efficiency analysis or mitigation.

Presentation has notable rough edges (e.g., typos such as 'recomended', garbled special characters in Table 7, formatting inconsistencies in equations), and code/dataset release is only promised 'upon publication', which weakens near-term reproducibility.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely new and under-explored task—reference-video-conditioned temporal effect transfer (Ref + Input → Output)—and the claim of being first on this V2V setup appears credible given the related-work coverage.

The dataset construction is the strongest contribution: a three-pronged pipeline (LoRA-derived I2V effects, a scalable pose-conditioned V2V pair-generation algorithm, and programmatic code-based temporal effects) yielding 120K+ triplets across 1,700 effects. The V2V pair-creation algorithm (first/last frame anchoring with intermediate pose conditioning) is a clever, reusable recipe for manufacturing motion-consistent edit pairs, which is the hardest data type to obtain.

The conditioning extension of Wan2.1 FLF2V (reference latents concatenated width-wise to both noisy and conditioning latents, hybrid masking) is a reasonable, well-motivated design, and Figure 5 explains the token accounting clearly.

Evaluation is appropriately dominated by a large human preference study (15,000+ annotations, 500+ annotators, 2AFC with bootstrap uncertainty), which is the right primary metric for this perceptual task; ablation against a No-Ref variant shows the reference signal genuinely helps (OM 67.2%).
The multi-directional classifier-free guidance scheme (Eq. 1) enabling independent control of input vs. reference adherence is a practical and well-presented inference-time contribution.
Limitations are candidly discussed, including failure cases (Fig. 9), human-centric data bias, and doubled inference cost.
weaknesses: A central concern is data circularity: the V2V training pairs are themselves produced by generative models (FLF2V interpolation, pose-conditioned Wan VACE), and a portion of the V2V validation set is generated by the authors' own pipeline and 'manually filtered' for quality. This risks (a) training on pseudo-labels that inherit upstream model artifacts, and (b) an evaluation set biased toward the authors' model's inductive biases. The paper provides no quantitative validation of pair quality (e.g., pose/identity consistency measurements of generated V, V' pairs).

The quantitative metrics are weak proxies. Embedding-similarity gains over baselines are small (e.g., I2V Ref Sim. 0.7378 vs. 0.7230), and the lower First Frame Sim. for the proposed method is attributed to baseline 'under-editing'—a plausible but unverified interpretation. No perceptual metric specifically measures temporal effect alignment (e.g., time-synchronized dynamics), so the quantitative case rests almost entirely on the user study.

Some user-study margins are modest: for neural V2V, IVA win rates are only 53.7–60.7%, and several results sit within a few points of chance given the 2–5% bootstrap deviations. The claim of 'large preference' overstates some of these results.

Missing comparisons: the paper argues no existing method can do this task, but per-reference finetuning baselines (Dynamic Concepts/grid-based LoRA, cited as [2,3]) could be run per-effect as an upper bound or reference point; their omission weakens the 'generalizes better than finetuning' narrative.

The title/abstract framing as 'tuning-free' is potentially misleading: the model requires large-scale training and LoRA fine-tuning of a 14B backbone; 'tuning-free' applies only in the per-instance sense. This should be clarified.

Reported capabilities are modest: 480p, 33 frames, 50 sampling steps, ~7 minutes per video on an A100, and dynamic degree for code-based effects drops substantially for the proposed method (0.143 vs. 0.190 baseline in Table 10), suggesting some temporal dynamics are muted.

Generalization claims rest on validation sets derived from the same generators (unseen LoRAs, novel prompts through the same pipeline, unseen hyperparameters), so 'unseen effect categories' may be narrower than implied.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed new task: transferring temporally evolving visual effects from a reference video onto an input video/image, a capability that text-only or keyframe-conditioned editors demonstrably lack. The authors appear to be first to systematically address this setting.

Substantial dataset contribution: over 120K (reference, input, output) triplets spanning 1,700+ effects, assembled from three complementary sources (LoRA-derived I2V, an automated V2V pair-generation pipeline, and programmatic/code-based effects). The V2V pipeline (Sec. 3.2.2, Fig. 4) is a clever, scalable construction that preserves motion consistency between input and edited pairs, and the programmatic subset provides reproducible, precisely controllable effects.

Sensible architecture design: extending the Wan2.1 FLF2V conditioning mechanism with width-wise reference latent concatenation and a hybrid preserve/edit mask is a natural, well-explained reuse of an established backbone; the training recipe (condition dropout for multi-directional CFG, retention of FLF capability) is thoughtfully constructed.

Thorough human evaluation: a large 2AFC user study (15K+ annotations, 500+ annotators, practice-trial calibration, bootstrap uncertainty) across three tasks and three criteria (RVA, IVA, OM), with the No-Ref ablation included. Win rates are consistently above chance with reported variability.

Useful controllability feature: normalized multi-directional classifier-free guidance (Eq. 1–5) enabling inference-time trade-off between reference-effect adherence and input preservation, with qualitative illustration (Fig. 8).
Honest limitations section (fine-grained occlusions, human-centric dataset bias, 2x inference cost) with a concrete failure example (Fig. 9); code and dataset release promised.
weaknesses: Circularity concern in the training data: the V2V pipeline relies on Qwen Image/Edit, Wan VACE-1.3B, and Wan FLF2V, and the LoRA subset is built on Wan 2.1 I2V. The model is thus substantially trained on outputs of the very (or closely related) systems used as baselines, raising questions about whether gains reflect genuine effect-transfer ability or distilled artifacts/biases of the generator models. The paper does not analyze this.

Missing ablation studies: there are no ablations over the three data sources (relative contribution of LoRA vs. neural V2V vs. code-based data), the conditioning architecture choices (width-wise concat vs. alternatives), mask design, or dataset scale. The only ablation is the No-Ref variant in the user study. These would significantly strengthen the scientific case.

Quantitative metrics are weak proxies: validation sets have no ground-truth outputs, so evaluation reduces to embedding similarities (VideoPrism/CLIP) and VBench-style statistics. Higher Ref Sim. could partly favor a model sharing the reference backbone; the paper itself concedes metrics only partially capture effect transfer. More targeted automatic measures (e.g., temporal-effect disentanglement checks, or metrics computed on the programmatic subset where ground truth exists) would be more convincing.

Some validation data is generated by the authors' own pipeline with novel prompts and then manually filtered for perceptual quality, introducing potential evaluator bias; the neural V2V validation set is small (100+ instances) and selection criteria are not fully specified.

Baselines are all text-conditioned variants that structurally cannot access the reference video; while this is inherent to a new task, comparisons against at least one reference-video-aware baseline (e.g., VACE with reference tokens repurposed, or Dynamic Concepts-style per-effect LoRAs) would better situate the contribution against the related work the paper cites.
Inference cost roughly doubles relative to the base model due to dual conditioning (7 min/video on an A100 at 480p, 33 frames); practical applicability at higher resolution/duration is untested.

Reproducibility depends on several large third-party systems (GPT-4o for effect prompts, Qwen, Wan) and curated LoRA lists; while the code-based subset is reproducible, the neural data pipeline's end-to-end yield/failure rates and filtering statistics are not reported.
